note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — GIANT JOINTED CANES
tiles.details: The locally archived Forest & Kim Starr Maui stand (panel 0) and Duarte Frade roadside stand (panel 1) show actual tall cane-like culms and long broad clasping leaves. Harry Rose's true attached flowering panicle (panel 4) shows the complete many-branched head. Recognize the large rhizomatous reed, but do not claim any ONE photo proves root-to-head linkage or Texas provenance. A permitted disturbed Texas specimen with roots/canes/head in one documented series remains desirable.
tiles.short: Robust rhizomatous reed, usually 2–6 m tall, with broad clasping leaves and a large terminal plume.
tiles.status: ACTUAL STAND AND COMPLETE HEAD PHOTOS PRESENT — TX SAME-PLANT SEQUENCE MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR
tiles.details: The Harry Rose Australian CC BY 2.0 macro (panel 3) genuinely shows a wide rounded clasping leaf base and a short membranous ligula-like flange with pale marginal hairs. Existing arrows mark the blade, clasping lobes and white hairs only. A physical 1-mm ruler and Texas voucher would let us measure its 0.7–2 mm literature ligule range, but the actual collar photograph does not include a reliable millimeter ruler. Phragmites can also have a ciliate membranous ligule; do not separate these reeds solely by visible fringe.
tiles.short: Rounded clasping blade base; a short ciliate membranous ligule, approximately 0.7–2 mm.
tiles.status: TRUE SPECIES COLLAR PHOTO PRESENT — 1-MM LOCAL SCALE AND PHRAGMITES MATCH MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE ONE MATURE SPIKELET AND ITS GLUMES
tiles.details: Open a mature attached spikelet under 10–20× and separate the TWO basal glumes from the several individual florets. Count glume veins and measure each part; do not call the entire multi-flowered spikelet one seed. These measurements are published botanical ranges, not dimensions established from the archived photos.
tiles.short: Spikelets about 8–15 mm with multiple florets; two persistent 3–5-veined glumes usually about 8–13 mm.
tiles.status: LITERATURE MEASUREMENTS — DISSECTION AND SCALE MISSING

tiles.heading: 04 · LEMMA SILK IS NOT A LONG AWN
tiles.details: Locate the hairy fertile lemma and its callus, then examine the apex for a short median awnlet between tiny teeth. The silky basal hairs are NOT awns. Most importantly, examine the rachilla between successive florets: Arundo lacks the long conspicuous silky rachilla hairs characteristic of Phragmites. The basal floret region can bear hair tufts, so do not oversimplify to 'every axis hairless'.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma roughly 6–12 mm; basal/back hairs 5–8 mm; short median awnlet usually 1–3 mm where present.

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS REED LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Confirm the hair origin in a mature Arundo/Phragmites spikelet pair, not merely a drooping plume or ciliate collar. Native giant cutgrass (Zizaniopsis miliacea) has cutting leaf margins and distinct reproductive units. Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) has sessile/pedicelled spikelet pairs. Native versus introduced Phragmites lineage is a separate determination and must not be inferred from reed appearance.
tiles.short: Phragmites: long silky rachilla hairs; giant cutgrass: different floral structure; Johnsongrass: paired sorghum spikelets.
tiles.status: TEXT COMPARISON READY — MATCHED TEXAS MACROS NEEDED

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND HANDOFF
tiles.details: CURRENT ROLE COVERAGE: FOUR original local photos (2 stand/growth views, true collar, complete attached plume), ONE newly linked JMK real photographed heavy woody RHIZOME under CC BY-SA 4.0; the rhizome remains external and not same-plant linked to a head. Required FINAL: local authenticated lower crown with connected cane and rhizome, calibrated true ligule (actual collar photo already exists), mature multi-flowered spikelet, separated glumes/lemma/palea, matched Phragmites rachilla-versus-lemma hair placement and on-page/mobile source/marker QA. Keep the original introduced/non-native status. No new JPEG bytes in repository and no new gross arrows.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — real rhizome reference, not a connected Texas voucher
tiles.status: GROWTH/REAL RHIZOME/TRUE COLLAR/HEAD DOCUMENTED SEPARATELY; MICRO-ANATOMY AND TX CONTINUITY PENDING

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the whole plant
steps.look_for: See the tall stand of stout, jointed, upright canes with wide green leaves. This tells you what giant reed looks like from several steps away.
steps.why_it_matters: This is your first clue, not proof: common reed and giant cutgrass can also form tall stands.

steps.title: 2 · Follow one leaf to its base
steps.look_for: Find where the broad leaf blade joins the wrapping sheath. Notice the rounded, clasping leaf-base shoulders and the pale, hairy-edged ligule (the tiny flap on the inside).
steps.why_it_matters: This close-up is a real Arundo collar with existing arrows. A hairy ligule by itself is NOT enough to separate the reeds.

steps.title: 3 · Look at the top of a flowering cane
steps.look_for: The flower head is a large branching plume made of many slender branches, each carrying tiny spikelets.
steps.why_it_matters: A flowering plume is useful, but both Arundo and Phragmites can have feathery heads. Inspect a spikelet next.

steps.title: 4 · See what is inside the plume
steps.look_for: The published photographic plate includes close views of true Arundo spikelets, glumes (the two scales at a spikelet's base) and individual florets (little flowers).
steps.why_it_matters: Arundo's conspicuous silky hairs are mostly associated with the florets/lemmas. Phragmites has long silky hairs along the spikelet axis (rachilla). The exact hair attachment in this plate is not yet verified at microscopic scale.

panels.label: GIANT REED — archived stand and broad leaves
panels.caption: Large reed canes with broad blades make a dense stand. Do not infer mature spikelet, collar, rhizome cut section or locality in Texas from this image.
panels.creator: Forest & Kim Starr
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: GIANT REED — real leaf collar, ciliate membranous ligule and clasping blade base
panels.caption: This is the actual junction of blade and sheath. The pale collar has rounded clasping lobes; a whitish CILIATE fringe extends from the membranous ligule inside. Do NOT teach that Arundo has a hairless ligule; some comparative literature describes the leaf collar differently. Use leaf-base shape as a supporting clue, then confirm spikelet anatomy.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: GIANT REED — actual tall upright branching flowering panicle
panels.caption: A complete flowering plume shows many slender side branches spreading off a central axis, with the overall panicle held upright. Panicle posture varies, so never separate giant reed from common reed by plume silhouette alone. Floret rachilla and lemma hairs cannot be seen at this magnification.
panels.creator: Harry Rose (Macleay Grass Man)

intro: Start with a whole plant. Then inspect the leaf base and flower head. The last picture shows the reproductive parts that help distinguish this grass from common reed.
memory_rule: Thick jointed canes → broad clasping leaves → upright branching plume → check the spikelet.
safety_note: If you only have an unflowered tall reed, use a tentative identification. Don't call it Arundo based on height or plume shape alone; compare the collar and mature reproductive parts.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

morphology.habit: Dense stands of tall cane-like stems; selected photograph shows a stand in Maui, not a Texas locality.
morphology.leaves: Broad flat grass blades on conspicuous culms; sheath and ligule require close photographs.
morphology.inflorescence: Large terminal panicle; panicle architecture and spikelet detail remain photo gaps.
